title: Gather All Components
description: Collect every component before starting. Verify quantities against this list.
instructions: 1x Raspberry Pi 5 (4GB or 8GB)
1x MicroSD card 32GB+ (Class 10 or better) OR NVMe SSD with Pi 5 M.2 HAT
1x Official Raspberry Pi 5 USB-C Power Supply (5V 5A)
1x PZEM-004T V3.0 AC energy monitor module
1x USB-TTL adapter (CP2102 or CH340 based, 3.3V logic)
1x YF-S201 water flow sensor (1/2 inch BSP, hall effect, 3-wire)
1x MQ-4 methane/natural gas sensor module (with onboard LM393 comparator)
1x ADS1115 16-bit ADC breakout board (I2C, 4-channel)
1x 5mm Red LED (standard through-hole)
1x 330 ohm resistor (orange-orange-brown bands)
1x 10k ohm resistor (brown-black-orange bands) — pull-down for YF-S201
1x 4.7k ohm resistor x2 — I2C pull-ups for ADS1115 SDA and SCL lines
1x Half-size breadboard (400 holes) or full-size breadboard
Jumper wires — male-to-female and male-to-male, assorted colours
1x Small project enclosure box (optional but recommended for installation)
Electrical tape, zip ties, heat-shrink tubing
Multimeter for continuity and voltage checks
warnings: NEVER connect the PZEM-004T to mains AC (230V) without proper electrical safety knowledge. If unsure, hire a licensed electrician for the AC side only.
The Raspberry Pi 5 uses 3.3V GPIO logic. Do NOT connect 5V signals directly to GPIO pins — it will damage the Pi permanently.
MQ-4 sensor requires 5V supply. Its analog output must go through the ADS1115, NOT directly to the Pi GPIO.

title: Flash the Operating System
description: Install Raspberry Pi OS on the microSD card or NVMe SSD.
instructions: Download Raspberry Pi Imager from raspberrypi.com/software on your laptop
Insert the microSD card into your laptop
Open Raspberry Pi Imager → Choose OS → Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit, Bookworm)
Click the gear icon (Advanced Options) before flashing:
- Set hostname: smartmeter.local
- Enable SSH with password authentication
- Set username: pi  |  Password: (choose a strong password)
- Configure WiFi: enter your home WiFi SSID and password
- Set locale and timezone to your region (e.g. Asia/Kolkata)
Click Save → Choose Storage → select your SD card → Write
Wait for write and verification to complete (~5 minutes)
Eject the card safely and insert it into the Raspberry Pi 5 SD card slot
warnings: Double-check you selected the correct drive before writing — it will erase everything on that drive.
Use a genuine high-quality SD card (SanDisk Endurance or Samsung Pro Endurance). Cheap cards corrupt under continuous database writes.

title: First Boot and System Configuration
description: Power on the Pi, SSH in, and enable the required hardware interfaces.
instructions: Connect Pi to power via USB-C. Wait 90 seconds for first boot to complete.
From your laptop terminal: ssh pi@smartmeter.local
If SSH connection fails, find the Pi IP via your router admin page and use: ssh pi@<IP_ADDRESS>
Once logged in, run the system update:
sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
Enable required interfaces via raspi-config:
sudo raspi-config
→ Interface Options → I2C → Enable → Yes
→ Interface Options → Serial Port → Disable shell on serial → Yes → Enable serial hardware → Yes
→ Finish → Reboot
After reboot, verify I2C is active: ls /dev/i2c*  (should show /dev/i2c-1)
Verify UART is active: ls /dev/serial*  (should show /dev/serial0 or /dev/ttyAMA0)
Install system dependencies:
sudo apt install -y python3-pip python3-venv git sqlite3 i2c-tools
warnings: Always disable the serial console (login shell) on the UART port before using it for PZEM-004T. Leaving the console enabled will corrupt Modbus communication.

title: Set Up Breadboard Power Rails
description: Connect the Raspberry Pi 5V and 3.3V power to the breadboard rails before connecting any sensors.
instructions: Place the breadboard on a stable surface next to the Raspberry Pi
Identify the Pi GPIO header — it is the 2x20 pin black connector on the board
Use the GPIO pinout (run 'pinout' command on Pi or visit pinout.xyz):
- Pin 2 or 4 = 5V power
- Pin 1 or 17 = 3.3V power
Connect a RED jumper wire: Pi GPIO Pin 2 (5V) → breadboard top positive rail (+)
Connect a BLACK jumper wire: Pi GPIO Pin 6 (GND) → breadboard top negative rail (−)
Connect a second BLACK jumper wire: breadboard top negative rail → breadboard bottom negative rail (bridge the two GND rails)
Connect an ORANGE jumper wire: Pi GPIO Pin 1 (3.3V) → breadboard bottom positive rail (+)
Now you have: top rail = 5V/GND for sensors needing 5V (MQ-4, YF-S201)
And: bottom rail = 3.3V/GND for sensors needing 3.3V (ADS1115)
Verify with multimeter: top (+) to top (−) should read 5.0V, bottom (+) to top (−) should read 3.3V
warnings: Do not mix 5V and 3.3V rails. Label them with coloured tape if needed.
Always measure voltages before connecting any sensor to avoid damaging the Pi.

title: Wire the ADS1115 I2C ADC
description: The ADS1115 converts the MQ-4 analog output to a digital I2C signal the Pi can read. Wire it first since other components depend on it.
instructions: Place the ADS1115 breakout board on the breadboard (straddles center gap, pins in rows e and f)
ADS1115 has these pins: VDD, GND, SCL, SDA, ADDR, ALRT, A0, A1, A2, A3
Power connections:
- ADS1115 VDD → bottom positive rail (3.3V) — RED wire
- ADS1115 GND → bottom negative rail (GND) — BLACK wire
I2C bus connections:
- ADS1115 SCL → Pi GPIO Pin 5 (BCM GPIO 3, I2C SCL) — YELLOW wire
- ADS1115 SDA → Pi GPIO Pin 3 (BCM GPIO 2, I2C SDA) — GREEN wire
ADDR pin: connect ADS1115 ADDR → GND rail (sets I2C address to 0x48)
ALRT pin: leave unconnected for this project
Add I2C pull-up resistors (if your ADS1115 breakout does NOT have them built in):
- 4.7kΩ resistor between SDA line and 3.3V rail
- 4.7kΩ resistor between SCL line and 3.3V rail
Note: most Adafruit/SparkFun ADS1115 breakouts have pull-ups built in — check your board
Verify I2C connection: on Pi terminal run: sudo i2cdetect -y 1
You should see address 0x48 appear in the grid
If nothing appears: check SDA/SCL are not swapped, check power connections
warnings: Do not connect ADS1115 VDD to 5V. The Pi I2C bus is 3.3V — using 5V will force 5V onto the Pi GPIO and destroy it.
If i2cdetect shows nothing, the most common cause is SDA/SCL swapped. Double check.

title: Wire the MQ-4 Gas Sensor via ADS1115
description: The MQ-4 detects methane and natural gas. Its analog output connects to ADS1115 channel A0.
instructions: The MQ-4 module has 4 pins: VCC, GND, DO (digital out), AO (analog out)
Power connections:
- MQ-4 VCC → top positive rail (5V) — RED wire
- MQ-4 GND → top negative rail (GND) — BLACK wire
Signal connection:
- MQ-4 AO (analog output) → ADS1115 A0 input — BLUE wire
Note: DO (digital output) is not used — leave it unconnected
IMPORTANT — Warm-up procedure:
The MQ-4 requires 24-48 hours of continuous power for the sensor element to stabilise
For the first power-on, run the sensor for at least 48 hours before trusting readings
The heater coil inside draws ~150mA from the 5V rail — this is normal
Calibration check:
In clean fresh air, the ADS1115 reading on A0 should be between 100–300 (raw ADC counts)
In presence of gas, the value will rise significantly (700–1000+)
Adjust the GAS_THRESHOLD in src/config.py to match your sensor's baseline
warnings: The MQ-4 heater gets warm to the touch — do not enclose it in an airtight box.
Never use the MQ-4 near an open flame. It detects combustible gas — if gas is present, do not create sparks.
The MQ-4 analog output is 0–5V. It goes to the ADS1115 input, NOT directly to the Pi GPIO.

title: Wire the YF-S201 Water Flow Sensor
description: The YF-S201 outputs a pulse train proportional to water flow rate. Each pulse represents approximately 2.25ml of water. Wire it to Pi GPIO 17 with a pull-down resistor.
instructions: The YF-S201 has 3 wires: RED (VCC), BLACK (GND), YELLOW (signal/pulse)
Power connections:
- RED wire → top positive rail (5V)
- BLACK wire → top negative rail (GND)
Signal conditioning — pull-down resistor:
- Place a 10kΩ resistor on the breadboard between two rows (e.g. rows 20 and 24, column c)
- Connect one end of the resistor to top negative rail (GND) — BLACK wire
- Connect the other end of the resistor to the YELLOW signal wire junction point
Signal connection to Pi:
- YELLOW signal wire → same breadboard row as top of pull-down resistor
- From that same row → Pi GPIO Pin 11 (BCM GPIO 17) — YELLOW wire
Note: the pull-down holds GPIO 17 LOW when no pulse is present, preventing false counts
IMPORTANT — Voltage divider required:
YF-S201 signal output is 5V. Pi GPIO is 3.3V tolerant maximum.
Add a voltage divider on the signal line:
- 1kΩ resistor between YF-S201 signal and GPIO 17
- 2kΩ resistor between GPIO 17 and GND
This divides 5V down to 3.3V safely
Alternatively use a 74AHCT125 level shifter for a cleaner solution
Physical installation:
- Install the YF-S201 inline on the cold water pipe feeding the flat
- Use PTFE thread tape on the BSP fittings to prevent leaks
- Ensure flow direction arrow on the sensor body matches water flow direction
warnings: CRITICAL: The YF-S201 outputs a 5V signal. Connecting it directly to a Pi GPIO without a voltage divider WILL damage the Pi. Do not skip the voltage divider step.
The sensor must be installed on the pipe before the flat's internal stop valve for accurate total consumption measurement.
Do not overtighten the BSP fittings — the plastic body can crack.

title: Wire the PZEM-004T Energy Monitor
description: The PZEM-004T V3.0 measures AC voltage, current, power, energy, frequency and power factor over Modbus RTU via UART. This is the most safety-critical step.
instructions: STOP — Read all warnings before proceeding with this step.
The PZEM-004T has two distinct connection sides:
SIDE A — Mains AC side (HIGH VOLTAGE): L (line/live), N (neutral), and current transformer clamp
SIDE B — Communication side (LOW VOLTAGE, safe): 5V, GND, TX, RX
LOW VOLTAGE communication connections (do these first, with power OFF):
- Connect USB-TTL adapter to the Pi: plug USB end into any Pi USB port
- USB-TTL RX → PZEM-004T TX — WHITE or GREEN wire
- USB-TTL TX → PZEM-004T RX — WHITE or GREEN wire (cross-connect)
- USB-TTL GND → PZEM-004T GND — BLACK wire
Note: the PZEM-004T V3.0 is powered from the AC side — do NOT connect 5V from Pi to PZEM
Verify USB-TTL adapter is detected on Pi:
ls /dev/ttyUSB*  → should show /dev/ttyUSB0
If not detected: sudo apt install -y cp210x-dkms (for CP2102 adapters)
HIGH VOLTAGE AC connections (hire a licensed electrician if not qualified):
- Turn OFF the main circuit breaker for the flat — verify with a non-contact tester
- Connect L (Live/Line, typically Brown wire in India) → PZEM L terminal
- Connect N (Neutral, typically Blue wire in India) → PZEM N terminal
- Clamp the current transformer (CT clamp, the donut-shaped coil) around the LIVE wire only
- Do NOT clamp both live and neutral inside the CT — it will read zero
- Connect the CT clamp cable to the PZEM CT input terminals
- Turn the circuit breaker back ON
- PZEM display (if fitted) should light up showing ~230V
warnings: CRITICAL: Mains AC (230V) is lethal. Never work on AC connections with power ON.
Always verify the circuit is de-energised with a non-contact voltage tester before touching any wire.
In India, the colour code is: Brown = Live, Blue = Neutral, Green/Yellow = Earth. Verify before connecting.
The CT clamp must encircle ONLY the live wire, not both live and neutral together.
If you are not a qualified electrician, stop here and hire one for the AC connections only. The Pi communication wiring is safe to do yourself.

title: Wire the Status Alert LED
description: A red LED on the enclosure indicates active alerts (gas leak, high consumption, anomaly detected).
instructions: Place the red LED on the breadboard — anode (longer leg) in column e, cathode (shorter leg) in column d of the same row band
Place the 330Ω resistor in series with the cathode:
- Resistor pin1 → same row as LED cathode (column c)
- Resistor pin2 → 4 rows down (column c)
Connect resistor pin2 row to GND rail — BLACK wire
Connect LED anode row to Pi GPIO Pin 13 (BCM GPIO 27) — RED wire
Note: GPIO 27 is a safe choice — it has no special boot function
Test the LED from Pi terminal:
python3 -c "import RPi.GPIO as GPIO; GPIO.setmode(GPIO.BCM); GPIO.setup(27, GPIO.OUT); GPIO.output(27, 1)"
LED should light up. Run again with GPIO.output(27, 0) to turn off.
Update src/config.py to set ALERT_LED_PIN = 27 if not already set
warnings: Always use a current-limiting resistor with an LED. 330Ω limits current to ~10mA at 3.3V — safe for both the LED and the Pi GPIO.
Do not use GPIO 2 or 3 for the LED — they are reserved for I2C.

title: Full Wiring Verification Before Software
description: Systematically verify every connection before powering on with sensors connected.
instructions: Power OFF the Pi (sudo shutdown -h now) and unplug USB-C power
Use a multimeter in continuity mode to verify each connection:
[ ] 5V rail to Pi Pin 2 — should beep
[ ] GND rail to Pi Pin 6 — should beep
[ ] 3.3V rail to Pi Pin 1 — should beep
[ ] ADS1115 VDD to 3.3V rail — should beep
[ ] ADS1115 SCL to Pi Pin 5 — should beep
[ ] ADS1115 SDA to Pi Pin 3 — should beep
[ ] MQ-4 VCC to 5V rail — should beep
[ ] MQ-4 AO to ADS1115 A0 — should beep
[ ] YF-S201 signal through voltage divider to Pi Pin 11 — should beep
[ ] LED anode through 330Ω to Pi Pin 13 — should beep (resistor in series, continuity ok)
[ ] USB-TTL RX to PZEM TX — should beep
[ ] USB-TTL TX to PZEM RX — should beep
Visual check — look for:
[ ] No bare wire ends touching each other
[ ] No jumper wires pulling pins at a sharp angle
[ ] MQ-4 module is not touching any metal surface
[ ] All breadboard jumpers are fully inserted (no half-inserted pins)
Power ON the Pi and run: sudo i2cdetect -y 1
Expected: address 0x48 visible (ADS1115)
Run: ls /dev/ttyUSB0
Expected: device exists (USB-TTL adapter for PZEM)
warnings: Never skip the verification step. A single wrong connection can destroy a GPIO pin or the entire Pi.
If i2cdetect shows 0x48 AND another address, the ADS1115 ADDR pin connection may be floating — tie it firmly to GND.

title: Deploy the Smart Meter Software
description: Transfer the project files to the Pi and install all Python dependencies.
instructions: From your laptop, copy the project to the Pi (replace IP with your Pi's IP):
scp -r ./smart_meter_project pi@smartmeter.local:~/smart_meter/
Or clone from a git repository if you pushed the code there:
git clone https://github.com/yourrepo/smart_meter.git ~/smart_meter
SSH into the Pi: ssh pi@smartmeter.local
Navigate to project: cd ~/smart_meter
Create a Python virtual environment:
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
Install all dependencies from requirements.txt:
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt
Copy and configure the environment file:
cp env.example .env
nano .env
Fill in your values:
MQTT_BROKER=your_mqtt_broker_ip
INFLUX_URL=http://your_influxdb_ip:8086
INFLUX_TOKEN=your_influxdb_token
INFLUX_ORG=your_org
INFLUX_BUCKET=smart_meter
TELEGRAM_TOKEN=your_bot_token
TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID=your_chat_id
FLAT_ID=flat_A
Save with Ctrl+X → Y → Enter
Run the application manually first to check for errors:
python3 smart_meter_all_in_one.py
Watch for startup messages — all sensors should initialise without errors
Open browser to http://smartmeter.local:5000 to verify the dashboard loads
Press Ctrl+C to stop
warnings: Never hardcode credentials in source files — always use the .env file.
If pip install fails on RPi.GPIO, run: sudo apt install -y python3-rpi.gpio first.

title: Configure and Enable the Systemd Service
description: Set up the smart meter as a background service that starts automatically on boot.
instructions: Copy the service file to systemd:
sudo cp smart_meter.service /etc/systemd/system/
Edit the service file to match your paths:
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/smart_meter.service
Verify these lines match your setup:
WorkingDirectory=/home/pi/smart_meter
ExecStart=/home/pi/smart_meter/venv/bin/python3 /home/pi/smart_meter/smart_meter_all_in_one.py
User=pi
Save and exit
Reload systemd and enable the service:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable smart_meter.service
sudo systemctl start smart_meter.service
Check the service is running:
sudo systemctl status smart_meter.service
You should see: Active: active (running)
View live logs:
sudo journalctl -u smart_meter.service -f
Test auto-start by rebooting:
sudo reboot
After 90 seconds, check: sudo systemctl status smart_meter.service
Dashboard should be available at http://smartmeter.local:5000 automatically
warnings: If the service fails to start, check logs with: sudo journalctl -u smart_meter.service -n 50
The most common failure is a wrong path in the service file. Double-check WorkingDirectory and ExecStart.

title: Calibrate the Water Flow Sensor
description: The YF-S201 emits approximately 450 pulses per litre but varies by unit. Calibrate for accuracy.
instructions: Get a measuring jug of known volume (1 litre or 2 litres)
Temporarily bypass the sensor by running water through it into the measuring jug
While water flows, record the pulse count from the Pi logs
Formula: PULSES_PER_LITRE = total_pulses / litres_flowed
Example: 900 pulses for 2 litres = 450 pulses/litre
Update src/config.py: FLOW_PULSES_PER_LITRE = <your measured value>
Restart the service: sudo systemctl restart smart_meter.service
Verify: run 1 litre through and confirm the dashboard shows 1.0L
Repeat 3 times and average the result for best accuracy
warnings: Do not skip calibration. Factory spec is 450 pulses/litre but individual sensors vary by ±10%.
Do calibration with the sensor installed in the pipe at operating water pressure — flow rate affects the calibration constant.

title: Calibrate the MQ-4 Gas Sensor Baseline
description: Establish the clean-air baseline for the gas sensor to prevent false alerts.
instructions: Ensure the MQ-4 has been powered for at least 48 hours before calibrating
Open a window — calibrate in clean, fresh air with no cooking or gas appliances running
Read the raw ADS1115 value from Pi terminal:

python3 -c "import board, busio, adafruit_ads1x15.ads1115 as ADS; from adafruit_ads1x15.analog_in import AnalogIn; i2c=busio.I2C(board.SCL,board.SDA); ads=ADS.ADS1115(i2c); ch=AnalogIn(ads,ADS.P0); print(ch.value, ch.voltage)"
Note the clean-air value (typically 0.1V–0.3V or 500–1500 raw counts)
Update src/config.py:
GAS_BASELINE = <your clean air reading>
GAS_ALERT_THRESHOLD = GAS_BASELINE * 3  (alert at 3x baseline)
Restart the service and confirm no false gas alerts appear
Test the alert by briefly holding the sensor near a small amount of gas (lighter gas, momentarily) — alert LED should light and Telegram message should arrive
warnings: Do not use a large amount of gas for testing — a brief sniff test with a lighter is sufficient.
If baseline is above 1.5V in clean air, the sensor may be faulty or still warming up. Wait another 24 hours and re-check.

title: End-to-End System Test
description: Verify all sensors, the dashboard, alerts, and AI features are working correctly.
instructions: Open the dashboard: http://smartmeter.local:5000
Electricity sensor test:
Turn on a known load (e.g. a 100W incandescent bulb or 1000W kettle)
Dashboard should show ~100W or ~1000W active power reading
Verify voltage reads ~230V and frequency ~50Hz
Water flow sensor test:
Open a tap briefly
Dashboard flow rate should spike then return to zero when closed
Daily consumption counter should increment
Gas sensor test:
Current gas level should show stable baseline value
No alert LED or Telegram message should be active
Alert system test:
Temporarily lower the gas threshold in config.py below current reading
Restart service — Telegram alert should arrive within 60 seconds
Restore threshold and restart
AI features test:
Let the system run for 1 hour collecting data
Check logs for anomaly detection output: sudo journalctl -u smart_meter.service | grep anomaly
Check predictive maintenance log entries
MQTT test:
On MQTT broker: mosquitto_sub -t smart_meter/# -v
Should see sensor readings published every 30 seconds
InfluxDB test:
Open your InfluxDB dashboard and verify data is appearing in the smart_meter bucket
Final check:
Reboot the Pi (sudo reboot) and confirm everything comes back automatically within 2 minutes
warnings: If electricity readings are zero, check the CT clamp is clamped around only the live wire and the clip is fully closed.
If MQTT is not publishing, check the broker IP in .env and that port 1883 is open on the broker firewall.

title: Permanent Installation and Enclosure
description: Mount the system permanently for long-term reliable operation.
instructions: Mount the Raspberry Pi and breadboard inside a ventilated project enclosure box
Drill ventilation holes on the sides of the box — the MQ-4 heater generates heat
Drill a hole for the MQ-4 sensor to face outward into the room air
Mount the enclosure near the electricity meter / distribution board — close to where you tapped the AC supply
Cable management:
Route the PZEM-004T AC wires inside conduit or cable trunking
Keep AC and DC wiring separated — at least 50mm apart
Use zip ties to bundle and secure all DC jumper wires inside the box
Label all wires at both ends with a label maker or coloured tape
YF-S201 installation on pipe:
Drain the pipe before fitting
Apply PTFE tape to threads — 5-6 wraps, clockwise direction
Hand-tighten then add 1/4 turn with a spanner — do not overtighten
Restore water supply and check for leaks at fittings
Power: plug Pi USB-C into a dedicated 5A USB-C power supply
Do NOT use a phone charger — they cannot sustain 5A and will cause brownouts
Backup: configure automated SQLite backup to a USB flash drive weekly
Add to crontab: 0 2 * * 0 cp /home/pi/smart_meter/data/smart_meter.db /media/usb/backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).db
warnings: The enclosure must be ventilated. A sealed box will cause the MQ-4 and Pi to overheat.
Keep the enclosure away from direct sunlight and sources of moisture.
In India, install a 1A fuse on the 5V DC supply line inside the enclosure as a safety measure.
Never mount the enclosure directly on or adjacent to the electrical distribution board — maintain at least 300mm clearance from high-voltage components.
